title: Parallel Quantum Advantage with Limited Adaptivity Requires Structure
abstract: Aaronson and Ambainis (Theory of Computing, 2014) conjectured that quantum query algorithms admit efficient almost-everywhere classical simulation: for any $T$-query quantum algorithm, its acceptance probability can be approximated on a $(1-δ)$ fraction of inputs, up to $ε$ additive error, using $\mathrm{poly}(T, 1/ε, 1/δ)$ classical queries. At a high level, the conjecture suggests that exponential quantum speedups are possible only on sufficiently structured inputs.   In this work, we make progress on this conjecture by proving it for quantum algorithms that make massively parallel quantum queries. In contrast, Yamakawa and Zhandry (Journal of the ACM, 2024) showed that quantum algorithms restricted to parallel queries can still achieve exponential speedups over classical algorithms for sampling problems. We establish our simulation theorem by proving the stronger statement that parallel-query quantum algorithms cannot distinguish the uniform distribution over oracles from oracles drawn from so-called "dense distributions". Our main technical contribution is a coupling theorem that relates the uniform distribution over oracles to oracles drawn from dense distributions.   We further extend this approach beyond the purely parallel setting, obtaining simulation theorems both for algorithms with a bounded quantum-query prefix followed by a massively parallel quantum-query stage, and for hybrid algorithms that make an arbitrary polynomial number of adaptive classical queries before the massively parallel quantum-query stage. Finally, using the parallel-query simulation theorem as a base case, we obtain simulation theorems for quantum algorithms with constant rounds of adaptivity.
summary: This work makes significant progress on the Simulation Conjecture by proving that quantum algorithms utilizing massively parallel queries can be efficiently simulated classically. The authors extend these results to handle limited adaptivity, providing strong theoretical bounds on when quantum speedups are achievable. This research deepens the understanding of the structural requirements necessary for genuine quantum computational advantage.
main_problem: The paper investigates the Simulation Conjecture, which posits that quantum query algorithms admit efficient classical simulation unless the input structure is highly specialized.
main_result: The authors prove simulation theorems for quantum algorithms involving massively parallel queries, extending results to algorithms with bounded adaptivity or polynomial classical preprocessing.
method: The core method involves establishing a 'coupling theorem' relating the uniform distribution over oracles to 'dense distributions,' allowing the simulation of quantum advantage claims.
model_or_system: The model is quantum query algorithms acting on boolean inputs, focusing specifically on the computational complexity derived from parallel query structures.
key_observables: Acceptance probability, error parameters (epsilon, delta), and query complexity (T).
important_parameters: The number of parallel query layers (d) and the degree of adaptivity (constant rounds or polynomial classical queries).
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon the Dense Indistinguishability Conjecture, which is used to bound the difference in success probabilities between uniform and dense oracle distributions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the structure of parallel query algorithms, showing the preparation stage, the massively parallel query stage, and the final measurement.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first tackling purely parallel query algorithms, then extending the simulation bounds to include limited adaptive quantum or classical prefixes, culminating in bounds for constant rounds of adaptivity.
why_interesting: While focused on query complexity, the rigorous mathematical techniques involving distribution coupling and simulation bounds are fundamental tools applicable to analyzing the complexity of quantum processes in general.
